questions.q: How does reconciliation differ from validation, according to this lesson?
options: Validation checks the correctness of what landed in a load; reconciliation checks completeness and accountability across the entire source-to-target picture
They are the same activity performed twice for safety
Reconciliation only applies to file migrations, never structured records
Validation happens after cutover, while reconciliation happens before it
questions.explain: Validation is about whether a load did what it was supposed to do. Reconciliation is broader — it asks whether every extracted record is accounted for as loaded, excluded, or rejected, end to end.

questions.q: In a complete reconciliation, what three buckets must every extracted record fall into, with the arithmetic closing exactly?
options: Loaded, deleted, and archived
Mapped, transformed, and sequenced
Successfully loaded, deliberately excluded by scope, or rejected and still needing resolution
Validated, spot-checked, and signed off
questions.explain: A real reconciliation accounts for every extracted record as loaded, excluded by a documented scope decision, or rejected — with extracted equaling loaded plus excluded plus rejected, nothing left unaccounted for.

questions.q: What does Bulk API 2.0 return once an ingest job completes, and why is it useful for reconciliation?
options: Only a single pass/fail flag for the entire job, with no per-record detail
A complete rollback of the job automatically if any record fails
A new sandbox automatically provisioned to investigate failures
Separate success and failure result sets with per-record status and, for failures, the specific error reason — directly usable as reconciliation raw material
questions.explain: Bulk API 2.0 returns per-record success and failure result sets with specific error reasons for failures, which is exactly the raw material a reconciliation report needs instead of guessing why records didn't load.

questions.q: A migration's failure result set shows a batch of records failed because they referenced an Account that hadn't loaded yet. What does this lesson say about reprocessing after the issue is fixed?
options: The entire original file must be re-run from scratch, including already-successful records
The failed-records result file can be corrected and re-processed on its own, rather than re-running the entire original file
Nothing can be done — failed records are permanently unrecoverable
The job Id must be discarded and the load started under a completely new scope
questions.explain: A practical benefit of Bulk API 2.0's result sets is that the failed-records file can be corrected and re-processed independently, without needing to re-run the entire original file.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say an unresolved discrepancy should block sign-off rather than being logged as a known issue to revisit later?
options: Because discovering a gap like missing Contacts after cutover, in a live production org, is a far more expensive and riskier place to find it than before sign-off
Because Salesforce automatically blocks sign-off on any migration with a discrepancy
Because logged issues are not visible to the project sponsor
Because discrepancies under 10% of total volume are never worth tracking
questions.explain: The discipline exists because 'later' means after cutover, in a live org — a much costlier and riskier time to discover a real gap than before sign-off, when it can still be fixed cleanly.
